Brickkiln
brĭk´kĭl
n. (the furnace in which bricks were burnt; a place of forced labour and of judgment; Hebrew malben)
English brick + kiln, from Latin culina, a stove. The Hebrew malben is the brick-mould or the place of brick-making — the tool and the yard together.

Biblical Definition

The brickkiln in Scripture is always bound up with bondage or judgment. David dealt so with the Ammonites: he “made them pass through the brickkiln” (2Sa 12:31). Jeremiah was told to bury stones “in the clay in the brickkiln, which is at the entry of Pharaoh's house in Tahpanhes” (Jer 43:9), so that Nebuchadnezzar's throne might one day stand on the very pavement where Judah's refugees had trusted Egypt. Nahum mocks Nineveh with it: “go into clay, and tread the morter, make strong the brickkiln” (Nah 3:14). Behind all of it stands Egypt, where they “made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in morter, and in brick” (Exo 1:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a brickkiln as a kiln or furnace in which bricks are baked or burnt, and a kiln as a fabric of brick or stone for the purpose of burning or drying.

expand to see more

BRICKKILN, n. A kiln or furnace in which bricks are baked or burnt; or a pile of bricks laid loose, with arches underneath to receive the wood or fuel.

BRICK, n. A mass of earth, chiefly clay, first moistened and made fine by kneading, then formed into a long square in a mould, dried and baked.

KILN, n. A fabric of brick or stone, which may be heated for the purpose of hardening, burning or drying any thing.

Key Scripture

2Sa 12:31 — "And he brought forth the people that were therein, and put them under saws, and under harrows of iron, and under axes of iron, and made them pass through the brickkiln: and thus did he unto all the cities of the children of Ammon. So David and all the people returned unto Jerusalem."

Jer 43:9 — "Take great stones in thine hand, and hide them in the clay in the brickkiln, which is at the entry of Pharaoh's house in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah;"

Nah 3:14 — "Draw thee waters for the siege, fortify thy strong holds: go into clay, and tread the morter, make strong the brickkiln."

Exo 1:14 — "And they made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field: all their service, wherein they made them serve, was with rigour."

Modern Corruption

Judah fled to Egypt for safety and Jeremiah buried stones in Pharaoh's brickyard to mark the spot where the conqueror would set his throne.

expand to see more

Jeremiah 43 is one of the bitterest ironies in the prophets. The remnant had been told plainly to stay in the land; they went down to Egypt instead, dragging Jeremiah with them, and the first thing God had him do on arrival was hide stones in the brick pavement at Tahpanhes and announce that Nebuchadnezzar would spread his royal pavilion over them. The refuge chosen against the word of God became the platform of the judgment they fled. Egypt is Scripture's standing name for that transaction — a house of bondage that always looks like shelter from a distance.

The corruption to name is the search for a political refuge from a spiritual verdict. Isaiah spent chapters on it: woe to them that go down to Egypt for help, and stay on horses, and look not unto the Holy One of Israel. The modern form is not usually a treaty but a strategy — the conviction that the church's safety lies in an alliance, a majority, or a technique, and that the word which called for repentance can be answered with a plan. Jeremiah's stones are still under the pavement of every such arrangement.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew malben (H4404), brickkiln, brick-mould; lebenah (H3843), a brick; chomer (H2563), clay or morter.

expand to see more

Hebrew malben (H4404) — brickkiln, brickwork; 2 Samuel 12:31, Jeremiah 43:9, Nahum 3:14.

Hebrew lebenah (H3843) — brick; Exodus 1:14, 5:7, Genesis 11:3.

Hebrew chomer (H2563) — clay, morter, heap; Exodus 1:14, Nahum 3:14, Isaiah 64:8.

Hebrew abodah (H5656) — service, bondage, labour; Exodus 1:14, 2:23.

Hebrew perek (H6531) — rigour, harshness; Exodus 1:14, Leviticus 25:43.

Usage

"“Hide them in the clay in the brickkiln” — a throne foretold in a brickyard."

"“Go into clay, and tread the morter” — Nahum's mockery of Nineveh's defences."

"“In morter, and in brick” — the bitterness of Egypt."
